config.prompt: A codified constitution is deliberately hard to change — the US kind needs approval by three quarters of the states for each amendment. How many amendments have made it through?
config.why: Twenty-seven — and the courts police the hierarchy: Marbury v Madison (1803) claimed and established judicial review, striking down statutes that conflict with the constitution.

activities.anchor: The United Kingdom is the great exception
activities.caption: pair each constitutional feature with its system
activities.name: slFrameMatch

config.prompt: Two constitutional pictures — pair the feature with the system it describes:

pairs.right: a single authoritative document, entrenched — amendable only by special procedure
no single document: statute law (Magna Carta 1215, Bill of Rights 1689, the Parliament Acts, the Human Rights Act 1998), common law principles and conventions
strikes statutes down against the constitution (Marbury v Madison, 1803)
tests ministers and regulations against statutes — no court can strike an Act down
the Human Rights Act 1998's remedy — the nearest thing to a constitutional check

config.why: Conventions — binding political customs like the royal assent convention — no court enforces but everyone obeys; and the system's genius and fragility is that Parliament itself is the ceiling.

activities.anchor: In a typical year Parliament passes
activities.caption: call the Act count behind the instrument flood
activities.name: slActsEstimate

config.prompt: Statutory instruments outnumber Acts nearly a hundred to one (about 3,000 annually). Roughly how many public general Acts does that make?
config.why: A few dozen — drafted with almost mathematical care, which is exactly why so much litigation is about what the words reach. The instruments get their own safeguards: affirmative or negative resolutions and a joint committee.

activities.anchor: This is the efficiency-versus-scrutiny trade-off in law's purest form
activities.caption: find the line that understates the binding force
activities.name: slDelegatedSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary goes beyond the grant — click it:
lines: An Act enables a minister, a local authority or the Crown to make delegated legislation — around 3,000 statutory instruments a year.
Parliamentary safeguards: affirmative resolution (active approval), negative resolution (stands unless objected to), plus a joint committee.
Judicial safeguard: an instrument beyond the parent Act's grant is ultra vires — void.
In 2021 the courts ruled pandemic procurement guidance beyond the Public Health Act powers it claimed.
A statutory instrument binds only advisory bodies — everyone else may ignore it.
config.correction: A statutory instrument binds exactly as an Act does in practice — it is simply vulnerable to being voided for going beyond its enabling power.
config.why: Delegation multiplies law-making power, so validity always traces back to the authority that was granted.

activities.caption: pair each reading rule with its case
activities.name: slInterpMatch

config.prompt: Four named approaches — pair each with the case that shows it:

pairs.right: Whiteley v Chappell (1908): impersonating a dead voter escaped "any person entitled to vote"
Adler v George (1964): convicted while already inside the "vicinity" of the prohibited station
Smith v Hughes (1960): balcony solicitation was "in a street" within the Street Offences Act 1959
Royal College of Nursing v DHSS (1981): nurses supervising early abortions as medicine moved on since 1967

config.why: The rules are not a code — the same case can be argued under two approaches, and the choice itself is the argument: literalism lets drafters' accidents defeat purpose; purposivism lets judges rewrite statutes. Both complaints are true, which is why the topic exists.

activities.caption: file each item by the force it carries
activities.name: slPrecedentBuckets

config.prompt: Stare decisis, sorted — file each item by the force it carries:

items.label: the ratio decidendi — the rule required to decide on the material facts
the UK Supreme Court over every court below it
obiter dicta — hypotheticals, commentary, extra reasons
distinguishing on a material difference of facts
overruling outright — the top court's Practice Statement 1966 permits it
the Young v Bristol Aeroplane (1944) escape hatches: conflicting decisions, per incuriam

config.why: Like cases decided alike delivers predictability, equality and efficiency in one rule — and the three lawful exits make precedent a system for managed change, not a straitjacket.

activities.anchor: The method's power shows in its landmarks
activities.caption: bet on what the Lords did with the fiction
activities.name: slLandmarkPredict

config.q: R v R (1991): the defence invokes the old fiction that a husband cannot rape his wife. What did the court do?
choices: Accepted the fiction — marriage is consent
Held the fiction an anachronism — judge-made change that Parliament then confirmed by statute
Struck the case out and left the matter to Parliament
config.why: The other landmark: Donoghue v Stevenson (1932) — the snail in the ginger-beer bottle, where no contract existed — generated the neighbour principle and with it the modern tort of negligence. Precedent builds the law incrementally, and statute ratifies or redirects it.

activities.anchor: But judicial precedent also governs the statutes themselves
activities.caption: drag the divider — builds, then revises
activities.name: slBraidedCompare

config.prompt: The two sources are braided, not parallel — drag the divider:

before.label: The common law builds
before.text: Donoghue's neighbour principle creates the modern tort of negligence (1932); R v R (1991) ends the marital-consent fiction — incremental, case by case.

after.label: Parliament revises
after.text: The War Damage Act 1965 reversed Burmah Oil v Lord Advocate — any common-law rule falls to clear words. Yet the reading rules that decide what the revision means are still the courts'.

config.why: One makes the law the other revises, and also supplies the reading rules that decide what revisions mean — a working lawyer rarely asks "which source applies?": usually both at once, one constraining the other.
